stem: A regression with 4 independent variables estimated on 40 observations has an R-squared of 0.64. The adjusted R-squared is closest to:

rationale.A: Incorrect. 0.640 is the unadjusted R-squared; it ignores the penalty for the number of variables.
rationale.B: Incorrect. 0.610 uses n − k = 36 in the denominator instead of n − k − 1 = 35.
rationale.C: Correct. Applying (n − 1)/(n − k − 1) = 39/35 to the unexplained share of 0.36 gives 0.599.

stem: An unrestricted model with 4 independent variables estimated on 40 observations has SSE = 180. A restricted model that excludes 2 of the variables has SSE = 210. The F-statistic for testing whether the two excluded coefficients are jointly zero is closest to:
explanation: F = [(210 − 180)/2] / [180/(40 − 4 − 1)] = 15/5.143 = 2.92. With a 5% critical F(2, 35) of about 3.27, the two variables are not jointly significant.

rationale.A: Correct. The increase in SSE per restriction (15) divided by the unrestricted MSE (5.143) equals 2.92.
rationale.B: Incorrect. 5.83 forgets to divide the increase in SSE by the number of restrictions, q = 2.
rationale.C: Incorrect. 2.50 uses the restricted model's SSE (210/35) in the denominator instead of the unrestricted SSE.

stem: Model X has AIC = 70.2 and BIC = 78.6. Model Y has AIC = 72.3 and BIC = 77.4. An analyst whose main objective is forecasting should most likely prefer:
options: Model Y, because it has the lower BIC
Model X, because it has the lower AIC
Model Y, because it has the higher AIC
explanation: Lower values are better for both criteria. AIC is the preferred criterion when the goal is prediction, so Model X (AIC 70.2) is chosen.

rationale.A: Incorrect. BIC is better suited to choosing the most parsimonious, best-fitting model, not to a forecasting objective.
rationale.B: Correct. For prediction, AIC is the preferred criterion and the lower value wins.
rationale.C: Incorrect. A higher AIC indicates a worse trade-off between fit and complexity.

stem: An analyst adds a fifth independent variable to a regression. R-squared rises from 0.640 to 0.645, and the new variable's t-statistic is 0.7. Compared with the four-variable model, the adjusted R-squared of the five-variable model will most likely be:
explanation: Adjusted R-squared increases only when the added variable's t-statistic exceeds 1 in absolute value. With |t| = 0.7, the penalty for the extra parameter outweighs the small gain in fit.

rationale.A: Correct. Because |t| = 0.7 < 1, adjusted R-squared falls even though R-squared rose.
rationale.B: Incorrect. A higher R-squared does not guarantee a higher adjusted R-squared; the degrees-of-freedom penalty dominates here.
rationale.C: Incorrect. Adjusted R-squared stays unchanged only in the knife-edge case of |t| exactly equal to 1.
